persons.name: Edward E Hunter
persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from death_notice, newspaper_1833_1835, poll_1834. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 6 August 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “E. E. Hunter” (f1839_v0227, printed page 42, ward 2, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Hunter' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins E. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 4 times, as “HUNTER EDWARD E”, “HUNTER E E”, 1834-11-15: 2 federal land entries — E2SW sec 02 T38N R14E; NE sec 13 T40N R13E, 320.00 acres stated in all, for $400.00 (ls0567, ls0568, ls0920, ls0919). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS COOK, UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. The register states this purchaser's residence as COOK, so the sale is contemporary evidence that a man of this name lived in Cook County on the date of sale. It is not evidence that he lived in the town. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: HUNTER EDWARD E matches Edward E Hunter: the forename names Edward E Hunter of the 4 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Hunter, Edward E.” (poll_1834_058, line 227). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Hunter' agrees with the entry's forenames; 4 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Hunter, Mrs. Electa | Letter. | November 3, 1848. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0654, printed page 191), admitted 1848-11-03 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Hunter' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins E. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print '• Hyde, Thomas S.' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 5 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. persons.name: Dr. Josiah C. Goodhue
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED MAN ON A RECONSTRUCTED ROOF. The papers name him and this household's dwelling does not: what is attested is the person and his trade, and what remains the reconstruction's is everything about where he lived. He is printed as 'Dr. Josian C. Goovnur' and the corpus reads his trade as physician. Cited at the Democrat of 4 February 1834, column 1. THIS ROOF DID NOT COME FROM HIS RECORD. The household was raised by the occupation census because the town of 3,265 people in 398 dwellings needed a physician and no documented one was available; the register (data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json, action `replace_invented`) is what says one now is. The dwelling's existence, position and footprint are unchanged and still conjectural, and nothing here claims he slept in it — only that the town's need for this trade is met by a man the papers name rather than by one this project invented. The invented name this record used to carry, and its name_basis block, are retired: an invented name is not kept beside a documented one. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1); the placement is L205. He is placed nowhere in particular by his own record, which is the condition of taking ANY roof of his trade — a man the papers put on a named street takes only a roof the plat stands on that street (T-0367), and one they place somewhere this scene cannot honour is refused outright. READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Goodhue, J. C.” (tax_1833_037, line 89); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Goodhue, J.” (poll_1834_044, line 213). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Goodhue' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 10 times, as “GOODHUE JOSIAH C”, “GOODHUE J C”, 1833-10-25 to 1836-06-30: 9 lots in the platted town — lot 10 of block 13 in the town the register codes CHIV (L10BL13CHIV, as printed); lot 13 of block 21 in the town the register codes CHIV (L13B21CHIV, as printed); lot 5 of block 13 in the town the register codes CHIV (L5BL13CHIV, as printed); lot 5 of block 17 in the town the register codes CHIV (L5BL17CHIV, as printed); lot 5 of block 37 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L5BL37CHIOT, as printed); lot 7 of block 38 in the town the register codes CHIOTV (L7BL38CHIOTV, as printed); lot 8 of block 13 in the town the register codes CHIV (L8BL13CHIV, as printed); lot 9 of block 13 in the town the register codes CHIV (L9BL13CHIV, as printed); lot 9 of block 51 in the town the register codes CHIOTV (L9BL51CHIOTV, as printed) and 1 parcel of the school section — lot 4 of block 119 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $17333.00 (ls0163, ls1169, ls1170, ls1171, ls1172, ls1173, ls1174, ls1175, ls1176, ls1177). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $17080.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: GOODHUE JOSIAH C matches Dr. Josiah C. Goodhue: the forename names Dr. Josiah C. Goodhue of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.
